questions.question_text: A dotplot is most appropriate for displaying:
questions.option_b: a small set of quantitative values
questions.explanation: Dotplots show individual quantitative values, good for small datasets. Pie charts show parts of a whole (categorical); two-way tables show two categorical variables.

questions.question_text: If you remove the largest value (an outlier) from a right-skewed dataset, the mean will:
questions.option_b: decrease
questions.explanation: Removing a large high outlier lowers the mean (which is sensitive to extremes). The median changes little, illustrating why the median is resistant to outliers.

questions.question_text: If the correlation between two variables is r = 0, this means there is:
questions.option_b: no LINEAR relationship (though a nonlinear one may exist)
questions.explanation: r = 0 indicates no linear association, but variables could still have a curved relationship. Correlation only measures linear strength and never proves causation.

questions.question_text: In the regression equation ŷ = 50 − 2x, a one-unit increase in x is associated with:
questions.option_b: a decrease of 2 in ŷ
questions.explanation: The slope −2 means ŷ decreases by 2 for each one-unit increase in x. A negative slope indicates an inverse relationship.

questions.question_text: Undercoverage bias occurs when:
questions.option_b: some groups in the population are left out of the sampling process
questions.explanation: Undercoverage happens when the sampling frame excludes parts of the population (e.g., a phone survey missing those without phones), biasing results. It's a sampling design flaw.

questions.question_text: A completely randomized design assigns treatments to subjects:
questions.option_b: entirely by chance, with all subjects equally likely to receive any treatment
questions.explanation: In a completely randomized design, random chance alone assigns treatments, balancing confounders. A randomized block design first groups similar subjects, then randomizes within blocks.

questions.question_text: Two events A and B are independent if:
questions.option_b: P(A|B) = P(A), meaning B's occurrence doesn't change A's probability
questions.explanation: Independence means knowing B occurred doesn't affect A's probability: P(A|B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive (P(A and B)=0) is different and implies dependence.

questions.question_text: If you flip a fair coin 3 times, the probability of getting exactly 2 heads is:
questions.explanation: Binomial: C(3,2)(0.5)²(0.5)¹ = 3 × 1/8 = 3/8. There are 3 ways to arrange 2 heads in 3 flips (HHT, HTH, THH), each with probability 1/8.

questions.question_text: The Central Limit Theorem becomes more applicable as:
questions.option_b: the sample size increases (commonly n ≥ 30)
questions.explanation: Larger samples make the sampling distribution of x̄ more normal, even for skewed populations. The n ≥ 30 guideline is when the CLT is generally considered to apply for means.

questions.question_text: Quadrupling the sample size will change the standard error of the mean by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Standard error is σ/√n; quadrupling n multiplies √n by 2, so the SE is halved (×1/2). Precision improves with the square root of sample size, not linearly.

questions.question_text: A confidence interval that does NOT contain a hypothesized value (like p = 0.5) suggests:
questions.option_b: the value can likely be rejected at the corresponding significance level
questions.explanation: If a value lies outside the interval, it's an implausible parameter value at that confidence level—equivalent to rejecting it in a two-sided test. Intervals and tests are linked.

questions.question_text: To estimate a proportion with a desired margin of error, using p̂ = 0.5 in the sample-size formula gives:
questions.option_b: the most conservative (largest) required sample size
questions.explanation: p(1−p) is maximized at p = 0.5, so using 0.5 yields the largest, safest sample size when the true proportion is unknown. It's the conservative planning choice.

questions.question_text: In a matched-pairs design, the analysis focuses on:
questions.option_b: the differences within each pair
questions.explanation: Matched-pairs (paired t) analyzes the differences within pairs as a single sample, controlling for variability between subjects. Treating the data as two independent groups would be incorrect.

questions.question_text: Increasing the sample size in a hypothesis test, holding other factors constant, will:
questions.option_b: increase the power (ability to detect a true effect)
questions.option_d: increase the Type I error rate
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce variability, making real effects easier to detect—higher power. Power also rises with larger effect size and higher α.

questions.question_text: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with k categories is:
questions.explanation: Goodness-of-fit df = number of categories minus 1 (k − 1). The independence/homogeneity test uses (rows−1)(columns−1) instead—match the formula to the test type.

questions.question_text: A chi-square test would be appropriate to analyze:
questions.option_b: whether favorite color is independent of gender (two categorical variables)
questions.explanation: Chi-square tests analyze categorical data—counts in categories. Comparing the distribution of one categorical variable across another (color by gender) is the independence test. Means use t-tests.

questions.question_text: A confidence interval for the slope that is entirely positive suggests:
questions.option_b: a significant positive linear relationship between x and y
questions.explanation: If the entire interval for the slope is above 0, you have evidence of a positive linear association. An interval containing 0 would mean no significant linear relationship.

questions.question_text: Degrees of freedom for inference about a regression slope with n data points is:
questions.explanation: Regression slope inference uses df = n − 2, because two parameters (slope and intercept) are estimated. This differs from the n − 1 used for a single mean.

questions.question_text: Standardizing data (computing z-scores) produces a distribution with:
questions.option_b: mean 0 and standard deviation 1
questions.explanation: Converting to z-scores rescales any distribution to mean 0, SD 1, enabling comparison across different scales. The shape of the distribution is preserved.

questions.question_text: A high r² value in regression indicates that:
questions.option_b: a large proportion of the variation in y is explained by the linear model
questions.explanation: r² is the fraction of the response's variability explained by the regression on x. High r² means a good linear fit—but it never establishes causation.

questions.question_text: Generalizing results to a population requires:
questions.option_b: random selection (sampling) from that population
questions.explanation: Random selection makes a sample representative, allowing generalization to the population. Random ASSIGNMENT (in experiments) supports causal claims—two distinct uses of randomness.

questions.question_text: The standard deviation of a discrete random variable measures:
questions.option_b: the typical spread of outcomes around the expected value
questions.explanation: The SD of a random variable quantifies how much outcomes typically deviate from the mean (expected value). It's the square root of the variance, Σ(x−μ)²P(x).

questions.question_text: The shape of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion is approximately normal when:
questions.option_b: np and n(1−p) are both at least 10
questions.explanation: The large-counts condition (np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10) ensures the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal, justifying normal-based inference for proportions.

questions.question_text: The critical value z* for a 95% confidence interval is approximately:
questions.explanation: 95% confidence uses z* ≈ 1.96; 90% uses 1.645 and 99% uses 2.576. Higher confidence requires a larger critical value and a wider interval.

questions.question_text: A one-sided (one-tailed) test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies:
questions.option_b: a specific direction (greater than OR less than)
questions.explanation: One-sided tests address directional alternatives (μ > value or μ < value), concentrating α in one tail. Two-sided tests check for any difference, splitting α across both tails.

questions.question_text: The chi-square distribution is:
questions.option_b: right-skewed, becoming more symmetric as degrees of freedom increase
questions.explanation: The chi-square distribution is right-skewed (only positive values) and approaches normality as df grows. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom.

questions.question_text: Which plot is used to assess whether the conditions for regression inference are met?
questions.option_b: a residual plot
questions.explanation: A residual plot reveals linearity (random scatter), constant variance (even spread), and outliers—key conditions for valid regression inference. Patterns signal violations.

questions.question_text: The mode of a data set is:
questions.option_b: the most frequently occurring value
questions.explanation: The mode is the most common value; the median is the middle; the mean is the average. A distribution can have one, multiple, or no modes.
